If this possessor brought witnesses that the person who sold it to him lived there even one day, etc. This is the Tur's view, that regarding the seller's one day of residence the purchaser cannot rely on migo and therefore requires witnesses. The Shach in seif katan 11 discusses this at length and writes that many disagree and that their view is more reasonable: the purchaser has a migo and is believed even without witnesses. I agree with him where the migo is that the field was never the challenger's. But where the challenger has witnesses that it was his, and the purchaser's migo is only that he could have claimed, "I bought it from you," it appears that even Tosafot agree he is not believed, because this is a migo involving brazenness. Although in many monetary matters we do accept a migo involving brazenness, here the migo is already weak, as the Baal HaMaor and Ramban explain at length. It is therefore enough to recognize such a migo where it does not also involve brazenness, but we should not recognize it where it does. This resolves Tosafot's wording. Rashbam writes that if one possessed for three years and claims, "I bought it from so-and-so, who had previously bought it from you," he is believed by migo that he could have said, "I bought it from you." Rashbam adds that the same applies if he has witnesses that his seller lived there one day. Tosafot write that Rashbam's words are correct where the challenger has witnesses that the land was his, but where there are no such witnesses, if the purchaser claims that he personally saw the seller buy it from the challenger, or that the seller lived there one day, he is believed by migo that it was never the challenger's even without having possessed for three years. The difficulty is obvious. Why do Tosafot say that Rashbam's words are correct when the challenger has witnesses? Even then, why should the purchaser need witnesses that his seller lived there one day? Why is he not believed by migo that he himself bought it from the challenger, just as he is believed when he says he personally saw the seller purchase it? Maharsha therefore writes that Rashbam's mention of witnesses is not exact and that the purchaser's own statement would suffice. That is very strained in Tosafot. The correct explanation is that when the purchaser says, "I personally saw my seller buy it from you," he can properly rely on the migo, "I myself bought it from you," because the level of brazenness is comparable in the two claims. But to say merely that the seller lived there one day, by migo that the purchaser himself bought it, is more brazen. Therefore he is not believed unless he has witnesses to the seller's one day of residence. Where the challenger has no witnesses at all that the land was his, however, the purchaser has the migo that he did not know it was ever the challenger's. There is no brazenness in that claim, and therefore he is believed regarding the seller's one day of residence even without witnesses. This is simple and clear in Tosafot, and should not be departed from, especially since the Baal HaMaor and Ramban in any event deny the migo in the stronger case. This also explains why the Tur rules that regarding one day of the seller's residence the purchaser's migo is ineffective, apparently against Tosafot, which is unusual for the Tur, particularly where the Rosh does not expressly disagree. According to what I have written, Tosafot themselves do not recognize a migo that the purchaser bought directly from the challenger for this purpose. The only migo they recognize is that the land was never the challenger's. The Rosh rejects that migo because the purchaser fears that witnesses may easily be found establishing the challenger's ownership, and therefore prefers a claim less vulnerable to direct contradiction. Once that migo is removed, Tosafot provide no basis for believing the purchaser without witnesses to the seller's one day of residence. The Tur therefore rules that witnesses are required. The Bach writes that a claim that the field was never the challenger's is itself brazen. I do not understand this, because the purchaser can say simply, "I do not know that it was yours." What brazenness is there in that? According to this distinction, namely that a migo of "it was never yours" may suffice while a migo of "I bought it from you" does not, even after three years of possession, one may ask from the Gemara in Ketubot. The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not teach a case where one says, "this field was yours and I purchased it from you," and answers that the latter clause involving witnesses cannot be established, because if he has a chazakah he should prevail, and if not, the result is obvious. Why not teach instead a case where he says, "this field was yours and I purchased it from so-and-so who lived there one day"? When there are no witnesses of prior ownership, he would be believed by the principle that the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted, but where the challenger has witnesses, even if the purchaser has three years of possession, this weaker migo should not suffice. This requires study.
For he has a claim together with his chazakah, etc. The phrase "for he has three years of chazakah" clearly indicates that the purchaser is believed specifically where he has a three-year chazakah and therefore a migo that he himself bought the land from the challenger. Where he lacks that migo because he did not possess for three years, and has only the migo that the land was never the challenger's, he is not believed. This also appears from the Rif. The Shach wishes to explain that the case is one where the challenger has witnesses of ancestral ownership, but this is strained. The entire passage addresses a case where the purchaser himself admits that the field belonged to the challenger's ancestors. Witnesses are nowhere mentioned. The Rambam expressly writes, "since he admitted that it was his," and then continues, "or he said that in my presence you sold it to him," showing that the case does not depend on outside witnesses. The Rif is even clearer. The reason appears as follows. Where the migo depends on the purchaser, who claims that he personally saw the seller purchase the field and would otherwise have the migo to deny the challenger's ownership, the Rosh's objection is compelling. This is a weak migo. The purchaser trusts his seller's statement that the seller bought from this challenger, and therefore does not wish to claim that the field was never the challenger's, because he suspects that the fact of the challenger's prior ownership is genuine and may easily be proved by witnesses. But whether the purchaser personally witnessed the seller's purchase is not something likely to be disproved by outside evidence. He may therefore falsely say, or mistakenly convince himself, that he personally witnessed the purchase. One cannot answer that this too can be disproved by witnesses who testify that the challenger never left their sight, as the Pilpula Charifta suggests. The purchaser is relying on the seller's assertion that the seller truly bought the field. If witnesses appear, the purchaser assumes they will confirm the sale, not disprove it. By contrast, the migo that the purchaser himself bought the property from the challenger is not weakened by the same fear. Even if witnesses later testify that the challenger was constantly with them, they would necessarily also know whether he sold the field to the seller. In any event, if the purchaser is contradicted on his direct-purchase claim, the field may still be established as belonging to the seller, from whom the purchaser has a deed, as Rashbam explains. The migo therefore remains meaningful. The more difficult case is where the migo belongs, conceptually, to the seller rather than to the purchaser. The purchaser says only that his seller told him he had bought from the challenger, and the challenger has no witnesses of prior ownership except the purchaser's admission. One can argue that had the seller himself been before us, he would have been believed by migo to deny that the field was ever the challenger's, and the Rosh's concern does not apply to the seller in the same way. If the seller is lying about having purchased the field, then the same witnesses who could disprove the challenger's title could also disprove the alleged sale. Why should one false claim be safer than the other? Thus, if the purchaser comes through the seller and merely repeats the seller's own account, perhaps we should advance for the purchaser whatever claim the seller himself could have made, since we generally advance claims for a purchaser. It is very strained to say, as the Pilpula Charifta does regarding the Rosh, that because the purchaser himself could not have successfully made this claim, we do not advance it for him on the seller's behalf. The entire point of advancing claims for a purchaser is to disregard the purchaser personally and ask what his predecessor could have claimed. The purchaser comes through the seller, and the rule that the first could convey only what he had should work in the purchaser's favor as well. For this reason Ri had to explain that the purchaser independently admits that he himself knows the field belonged to the challenger. Then the case is one of certainty against uncertainty. The challenger has definite prior title, while the purchaser's derivative claim is uncertain. One might object that when the purchaser says, "I personally saw the seller buy it from you," his claim too is definite. But we do not believe that statement independently; it is believed only by virtue of a migo, and here the migo fails for the reasons stated. Thus the purchaser remains in the category of uncertain claim against definite title. This appears to me to resolve the Rif and Rashbam according to Ri's approach. According to the Rambam, one need not rely on the definite-versus-uncertain principle. One can instead use Tosafot's explanation that where the purchaser himself is effectively one witness to the challenger's ownership, the seller's theoretical migo is ineffective because the purchaser would not accept the seller's denial. Even where the purchaser says he personally saw the sale, the seller has no migo to deny the challenger's ownership, because the purchaser would then see that his seller is lying and would not stand by him. When the seller claims the purchase occurred in the purchaser's presence, however, the purchaser is already inclined to believe his seller and may be mistaken in his certainty. But if the seller now denied the challenger's title entirely, the purchaser would recognize the contradiction and turn against him. There is also an aspect of migo involving two persons, since seller and purchaser would have to coordinate their positions. Tosafot's reasoning is thus sound. According to Ri, however, who grounds the rule in definite versus uncertain, the explanation above is necessary: because the purchaser is not independently believed that he personally saw the sale, his position remains uncertain. This is somewhat strained, especially since the Rosh's words in the name of Rashbam appear to say the opposite. The Rosh writes that if the purchaser had claimed, "I bought it from you," or "in my presence my seller bought it from you," he would be believed by the principle that the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted, since the challenger has no witnesses of prior ownership. This necessarily refers to a case without three years of possession, because with such possession the purchaser would be believed even where the challenger had witnesses. Rashbam's own language at the end of the Gemara also indicates that where the purchaser knows whether the seller bought the field, he is believed. Rashbam writes that in the case at hand, even if witnesses came establishing that the seller lived there one day, it would not help if they did not know whether he had purchased it, because there was no three-year possession. The implication is that if the purchaser himself knows that the seller purchased it, he may be believed by migo that the field was never the challenger's, giving a definite claim against a definite claim, as the Shach argues. It is possible, however, that the Gemara text should read "they do not know" rather than "he does not know," referring to the witnesses. That would remove the Shach's inference. The Tur therefore requires explanation. The Derishah discusses the matter at great length without reaching a clear resolution. It appears that the Tur understood the Rosh's initial presentation of Rashbam only according to the earlier assumption that Ri's entire rule depends on definite versus uncertain. On that assumption, where the purchaser has a definite claim that he personally witnessed the sale, the migo would indeed suffice. But after the Rosh explains Rashbam's position by saying that the migo that the field was never the challenger's is weak because the purchaser fears contrary witnesses, the same weakness applies even to the purchaser's claim that he personally witnessed the sale, unless he has the stronger migo based on three years of chazakah that he himself bought from the challenger. Thus, in the Rosh's final view, even Rashbam requires the stronger form of migo. The Tur therefore rules accordingly. The Shach further argues at length that if there are witnesses that the seller lived there one day, then even where the purchaser lacks three years of chazakah and does not claim that he personally saw the seller buy it, he should nevertheless be believed, because we advance for a purchaser whatever the seller could have claimed. He cites Ramban's proof from one who deposited property with another before witnesses and died, where we advance for the heirs whatever their father could have claimed by migo of return. The Shach distinguishes that there it is certain the object came to the heirs from their father, whereas here who says that the purchaser acquired the field from the particular person who lived there one day? If the purchaser has proof that he acquired it from that person, the Shach agrees with Ramban's law. I do not understand this distinction. The purchaser has a migo that the field was never the challenger's. When he instead says, "yes, it was yours, but I bought it from so-and-so, and that person lived there one day," why should he not be believed by the same migo? Rashbam's wording seems to support the Shach, because Rashbam infers from the purchaser's failure to say, "and I possessed it for three years," that the purchaser had a deed from the seller. Rashbam does not say that the purchaser would simply have been believed by migo that the field was never the challenger's without needing a deed. This indicates that Rashbam too does not recognize the migo in that form. Still, Rashbam may follow either the Rosh, that the migo "it was never yours" is weak because the prior ownership can be proved, or the view that a migo involving brazenness is not accepted. The case may be one where the challenger knows that the purchaser himself knows the field was his, so denying prior ownership would be brazen. But the Shach rejects the Rosh's approach and generally accepts a migo involving brazenness. It is therefore difficult to understand his distinction between proof of the transaction and a definite derivative claim. In truth, I already discussed above in siman 72 seif 1 that this general rule is disputed by the authorities. Even those who there recognize the derivative claim may have spoken only about movables, which are fully in the current holder's possession. Land remains in the chazakah of its original owner, and the purchaser's present possession, especially before three years, is not complete. His migo therefore resembles a migo used to extract. One should not simply equate the law of movables and land here. Since major authorities disagree, this remains a doubt of law, and the land should remain with the prior owner. This appears clear.
But if he merely said, "I purchased it from so-and-so," etc. The Shach in seif katan 15 holds that initially the possessor must have said, "I bought it from so-and-so, who bought it from you." Only then may he later explain his words and say that by "who bought it from you" he meant that the purchase occurred in his presence. But if he initially said only, "I bought it from so-and-so," how can he later add this new assertion where he has no migo? The Shach writes correctly. However, the Shach supports himself from Tosafot and appears to understand that Tosafot agree with this rule. That is not so. Tosafot disagree here with Rashbam and the Rosh. In the underlying case, Rashbam's text does not say that the seller told the purchaser that he had bought it from the challenger. Rashbam's version is simply, "I bought it from so-and-so, who had bought it from you," and Rashbam explains: meaning, the seller told me that he had bought it from you. Thus the Gemara itself does not say that the seller made that statement. Rashbam therefore writes that if the purchaser later explains, "he bought it from you in my presence," he is believed by migo. Rashbam thus agrees with the Rosh that one may explain one's earlier words. Tosafot, by contrast, although they cite Rashbam's formulation, write: "but now that he said, I bought it from so-and-so who bought it from you, and thereby admitted that it had been yours, he cannot later claim, he bought it from you in my presence," because that would be a retrospective migo. Thus even with this formulation Tosafot do not permit him to repair his claim afterward. Their disagreement with Rashbam is precisely whether such a later explanation is treated as merely clarifying the first statement or as a retrospective migo. Tosafot say the same explicitly in the case of the man who lived in the upper room. The Gemara says that had he claimed from the outset, "in my presence he bought it from you," he would have been believed. Tosafot explain that this does not mean he remains able to make that claim later by migo. Rather, only had he made that claim initially would he have been believed. This is expressly contrary to the Rosh, who holds that where the original wording was, "I bought it from so-and-so who bought it from you," and not, "he told me that he bought it from you," the purchaser may still clarify that he meant, "he bought it in my presence." This also explains the dispute in Ketubot concerning the old woman who said, "I seized them during his lifetime." Tosafot write that she is not believed by migo that she could have said she seized them during his lifetime, because that would be a retrospective migo. The Rosh, however, establishes the case where there are witnesses who saw the property and witnesses to the deposit, thereby removing the migo altogether. Why did the Rosh need this additional factual assumption? Because he follows his own view that a person may clarify an earlier statement. She could explain that when she said, "I seized them during his lifetime," she meant, "he demanded them from me during his lifetime and I did not return them." Tosafot, who do not allow such reinterpretation, can rely simply on the retrospective-migo problem. This is clear, and I wrote similarly above in siman 64. It therefore follows that the Shach's ruling itself is certainly correct. Since Tosafot in any event reject the Rosh's broader rule allowing later clarification, once we rule like the Rosh we should at least limit the principle to a case where the later words genuinely explain and follow from the earlier ones. We should not permit a claimant to add a wholly new fact to an earlier statement that was entirely silent about it. Consider this carefully.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: שאם שהה וכו' לא עלתה כו' הטעם דיכול המחזיק להתנצל חשבתי שחזר ממחאתו כיון דשתק ג"ש ולכן לא נזהרתי בשטרי סמ"ע ופשוט:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: If she and so on didn’t get the taste of the peddler to apologize, I thought he had come back from his illness as an armored jackpot and therefore I wasn’t careful with a simple and simple barter:

mechaber.he: אם עמד המוכר בדין עם המערער קודם שמכרה למחזיק ונפטר ממנו כיון שלא היו לו עדים שהיתה שלו אע"פ שלאחר שמכרה לזה המחזיק ערער עליו המערער והודה לו שהיתה שלו על פי המוכר שאמר לו שהיתה שלו וקנאה הוא ממנו לא הפסיד בזה כיון שכבר יצא זכאי מב"ד המוכר שמכרה לו:
mechaber.en: If the seller stood with the appellant before selling to the holder and was dismissed from him because he had no witness that he had been a lawyer who had sold him to the appellant and confessed that he was his according to the seller who told him that he was his and jealous he had not lost it because he had already been entitled to the familiar lawyer

beer_hagolah.he: שם סכ"ו
beer_hagolah.en: There's a cheque

beur_hagra.he:
אם עמד. ר"ל אפילו שלא החזיק הלוקח ג"ש דע"כ דר המוכר בו יום א' דאל"כ האיך זכה המוכר:
(ליקוט) אם עמד כו' יבמות פ' החולץ כר' אבא דאמר דקם דינא וקי"ל שם כמותי דפליגי בפלוגתא דאדמון ורבנן וכמ"ש הרי"ף שם וע"ל סי' לג סי"ב בהג"ה מיהו כו'. (ע"כ):
beur_hagra.en:
If he remained. Even if the purchaser did not possess it for three years, the seller must have lived there at least one day, for otherwise the seller could not have acquired it.
If he remained, etc. Yevamot, chapter HaCholetz, follows Rabbi Abba that the original judgment stands. The halakha follows him, as Rif explains. See siman 33:12 in the gloss.

meirat_einayim.he: ונפטר ממנו כיון כו'. פי' נפטר בטענת שלך היתה וקניתיהו ממך דנאמן במיגו דלא הי' שלך מעולם וכנ"ל:
meirat_einayim.en: And we'll get rid of him as John. P. died in your claim, and you bought an artist from you in your DNA from the world of your own DNA:

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: ונפטר ממנו פי' נפטר בטענת שלך היתה וקניתיה ממך דנאמן במגו דלא היה שלך מעולם [סמ"ע]:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: And we’ll get rid of him, according to your claim, and you’ve bought an artist from you in his body and has never been yours

urim_vetumim_urim.he: אם מחמת טענה וכו' כן הוא לשון הגמרא וטור כתב וז"ל והרמ"ה חילק בדבר וכתב היינו דוקא שמוכח מתוך השנים שמבטל הראשונה כגון שטען בשנים שמעיקרא כשירד המחזיק בתוכה ירד בה בטענת שטען עתה כו' ע"ש ועד"ר שם כתבתי דאפשר דהרא"ש שהביא הטור מודה לרמ"ה סמ"ע:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: If because of a claim, etc. The Gemara states the rule generally. Tur cites Rabbi Meir HaLevi Abulafia as distinguishing: it applies where the later claim is shown by its content to replace or explain the earlier one, such as where the possessor originally entered under the very basis now asserted. See Tur. Sema writes that Rosh may agree with this limitation.

mechaber.he: הביא המחזיק עדים שדר בו המוכר יום אחד ואחר כך הביא המערער עדים שהמחזיק רצה לקנותה ממנו וטוען אילו קניתיה מפלוני כמו שאתה טוען למה רצית לקנותה ממני אינה טענה שאומר רציתי לפייסך במעט מעות כדי לסלק תרעומתך (אבל אם לא טען הוא לא טענינן ליה) (ב"י בשם הרמב"ם בסו' ה"ט):
mechaber.en: The holder brought witnesses to the seller one day, and then the appellant brought witnesses that the holder wanted to buy it from him, claiming that I had bought it from Paluni as you claim what you wanted to buy from me was not a claim that I wanted to give you a bit of trouble to remove your complaint (but if he didn't claim he wasn't interested in me)

baer_hetev.he: אבל. נרא' דה"ט דאין אדם רגיל להוציא מעותיו בכדי. שם:
baer_hetev.en: But. Rath de R. D.C. has no ordinary man to remove his mitzvot. Name:

beer_hagolah.he:
שם סכ"ח עובדא לקמיה דרבא שם בבא בתרא ד"ל ע"ב וכמו שפירשו הרא"ש שם בפסקיו:
שם בגמרא דעביד אינש דזבין דיניה:
beer_hagolah.en:
There, seif 28, from the incident before Rava, Bava Batra 30b, as Rosh explains it in his rulings.
In the end of the day, Isaac was quoted as saying:

beur_hagra.he: אבל אם. שם מ"א א':
beur_hagra.en: But if. Name of A:

meirat_einayim.he: אבל אם לא טען לא טענינן ליה נראה דה"ט משום דאין אדם רגיל להוציא מעותיו בכדי ומטעם זה נמי בדין שכ' בסי"ח אם הביא המחזיק ראיה שהמערער א"ל לקחנו מהמוכר גם שם צריך המערער לטעון בעצמו עביד אינש דזבין דינא וכמ"ש בפרישה ולא טוענין כן עבורו כיון שרצה המערער להוציא ממון משא"כ במציעתא בהביא המחזיק עדים שיעצו המערער לקנותו לו דשם טוענין עבור המערער דיעצו כן משום דהוא נוח לו יותר מ"ה מסיק הטור והמחבר שם וכתבו דאם כופר ואומר מעולם לא יעצתיך כו' מחייבים להמערער דמשמע הא אינו כופר אף שאינו נותן טעם למה יעצו אנן טוענין עבורו ודו"ק:
meirat_einayim.en:
But if he didn't say anything to him, he would see that he was not an ordinary man to take his hands away, and that he had to say that he had no idea that he would have given him that he would not be able to do so, and that he would not give him any evidence that he would be able to do so
He is interested in him and DCO:

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: לא טענינן ליה ונראה דמ"מ ליורשים טענינן דומיא דטענת משטא דסי' פ"א לא טענינן ליה וליורשים טענינן:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: We do not plead this for him. Nevertheless, it appears that we do plead it for heirs, just as in siman 81 we do not advance the claim of jesting for the litigant himself but do advance it for his heirs.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: לא טענינן משום דאין אדם רגיל להוציא מעותיו בכדי [סמ"ע] וע"ב דמ"מ ליורשים טענינן:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: There is no ordinary man to take his hands away from him, and he does not care for him

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: אבל אם לא טען הוא לא טענינן ליה הם דברי הרמב"ם ולפי הנראה מדברי המ"מ יליף אותו הרמב"ם מהא דבגמרא אמינא אמר ליה אזבין דינא משמע דוקא דקאמר הכי אבל אנן לא טענינן. אך לפ"ז אף בהאי עובדא הנזכר בסעיף אחר זה דיעצהו ליקח נאמר גם כן בגמרא אמר ליה השני נוח לי והראשון קשה הימנו יהיה ג"כ צריך לטעון וזה לא נזכר ברמב"ם ובדברי הרמ"א כלל וכמ"ש הסמ"ע בס"ק ל"ג ע"ש. ולכן נרא' דהוציאו הרמב"ם דהך טענה גרוע היא מהא דאמרינן עבידו דקרו לשני טובא שני חזקה דאמרינן וה"מ שבע אבל שית אין לך מחאה גדולה מזו והקשו התוס' הא יש לו מיגו דזבניה ניהליה מקדם לקניינו במגו דזבנתי ממך ותי' הטור לקמן אות ל"ב דאין זה מגו דלא ידע אם יש לזה שטר אם יאמר שלקחה הימנו יתבענו המוכר לדין עכ"ל וקשה הא יכול לטעון ממוכר אח"כ זבינתי ממך ואכלתי שנין חזקה וא"כ הרי בטוח מכל אם יברר זה שטרו הרי טוען שלקחה הימנו ואם לא יברר מ"מ אין למוכר עליו שהרי טוען שגם מן המוכר לקח. והא לא קשי' איך יתכן שלקחת מן המוכר וכן מן הלוקח הא לא קשיא עביד אינש דזבין דינא וכמו שאמרו כאן וע"כ צריך לומר דזה לקנות הדבר פעמיים טענה גרוע היא ולא שכיח כלל ולכך לא אמרינן בי' מגו דהוי מילתא דלא שכיח ולא אמרינן בי' מגו כנודע ולפי זה אף אנן לא טענינן ליה כיון דהוא גרוע ולא שכיח דלא נימא גביה מגו איך נטעון אנן ופשוט. ודברי הרמב"ם מוכרחים ודוק. ולכך בהך עובדא דיעצהו לקנות והטענה השני נח ליה וכו' כיון דלא מצינו בגמרא ראייה דהוי טענה גרועה אף אנן טענינן ליה ובפרט דיש לחלק בסברא דבשלמא בנדון זה אמרינן אלו היה באמת טעמו למזבין דדינא ה"ל לטעון כן כיון דכך היה מחשבתו מתחילה ומדלא טען ש"מ דלא לזה נתכוון מה שאין כן בהך דיעצהו לקנות וכו' אין ראייה דאם כוונתו היה לכך למה לא טוען בבית דין דבוש הוא לטעון כן בבית דין כי ודאי נבלה עשה כמה שכתב הסמ"ע ס"ק ל"ט עיין שם ובכלל משגה עור בדרך ולכך מערים להסתיר ערמתו וא"ש:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: But if he did not make this claim himself, we do not make it for him. These are the Rambam's words. The Maggid Mishneh appears to understand that the Rambam derives this from the Gemara's wording, "I say that he told him, I bought the litigation," implying that only where the litigant himself says so may the explanation be accepted, but beit din does not make the claim for him. If that were the source, however, the same should apply in the following case where the challenger advised the possessor to purchase the field. There too the Gemara says that the challenger himself answered, "the second person is more convenient for me and the first is more difficult." One would then expect the Rambam and Rama to require that he actually make that claim. Yet no such requirement is stated, as the Sema observes in seif katan 33. It therefore appears that the Rambam derives his rule from the weakness of the present claim itself. The Gemara says that people sometimes purchase their own litigation, meaning they buy a disputed property merely to avoid legal trouble. Yet in the later discussion of one who had consumed for many years, the Gemara says that seven years suffice but six do not, because the challenger's deed is the strongest possible protest. Tosafot ask why the possessor should not be believed by migo that he bought the land from the challenger before the challenger's acquisition. The Tur later answers that this is not a valid migo because the possessor does not know whether the challenger holds a deed. If he were to say that he purchased from the challenger, the seller could sue him. But why can the possessor not say instead: I first purchased it from the seller and afterward purchased it again from the challenger, and I possessed for three years? This would protect him in either event. If the challenger produces a deed, the possessor claims a later purchase from him. If no deed is produced, the original seller cannot complain, because the possessor maintains that he also purchased from the original seller. Nor is it impossible for someone to purchase the same property twice. The Gemara itself says that a person may buy litigation simply for peace of mind. We must therefore say that purchasing the same property twice merely to settle competing claims is an unusually weak and uncommon explanation. Because it is not a normal occurrence, it does not generate a migo. We do not rely on a migo based on a highly uncommon claim. Once that is so, beit din likewise should not advance such a weak and unusual claim for a litigant who did not make it himself. The Rambam's ruling is therefore compelled. By contrast, in the case where the challenger advised the possessor to buy, and then explains, "the second person was more convenient for me than the first," the Gemara gives no indication that this is an inherently weak claim. Beit din may therefore advance it where appropriate. There is also a logical distinction. In the present case, if the possessor's actual intention had truly been to buy the litigation, he should naturally have said so when litigating. His failure to do so suggests that this was not his reason. In the advice case, however, even if that was the challenger's true motivation, he may be embarrassed to say openly in beit din that he deliberately manipulated another person into buying disputed property. As the Sema writes in seif katan 39, such conduct is improper and resembles placing a stumbling block before the blind. He may therefore conceal the embarrassing explanation unless prompted. This resolves the distinction.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: אבל כשמכרם הראשון וכו' אין צריך למחות דברים אלו המה תשובת רשב"א ועיין תומים כי הבאתי דבריו וכל ראייתו שמביא לדינו מגמרא ההיא דדר בקשתא ד' שנין וכו' וכן מהא דאמרי' וה"מ דאכלה שבע אבל שש לא ע"ש באריכות והוכחתי דס"ל כהי"מ דהביא הרשב"ם וכן דעת רז"ה דלכך צריך למחות כל ג"ש כדי שלא יטעון לאחר מחאה מכרת לי ובזה תרצתי לרשב"א על הנכון שלא יקשה עליו הקו' שהק' המהרי"ט ח"מ סימן כ"ו ע"ש באריכות אבל על המחבר צע"ג דהעתיק דינא דהרשב"א הנ"ל להלכה מבלי חולק והרשב"א ס"ל כהי"מ של רשב"ם והמחבר גופיה פעמים שונים בסימן זה סתם דלא כי"מ וכן ס"ל הרשב"ם והרמב"ן והרא"ש והנ"י וכן מוכח מתוס' וא"כ צע"ג שהעתיק להלכה דברי רשב"א:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: But when the first one sold it, etc. One need not protest. These are Responsa Rashba's words. See Tumim. I showed that Rashba's proof depends on the view that a new protest is required every three years so the possessor cannot later claim, 'After your earlier protest you sold it to me.' This is one of the interpretations cited by Rashbam and also followed by Rabbi Zerachiah HaLevi. That explains Rashba and answers Maharit. But Mechaber's adoption of Rashba without qualification is difficult, because Mechaber repeatedly rules against that interpretation in this siman, following Rashbam, Ramban, Rosh, Nimukei Yosef, and apparently Tosafot. The Shulchan Aruch's ruling therefore requires study.

mechaber.he: אם לא הביא המחזיק עדים. שדר בו המוכר יום אחד וטוען המערער שהמוכר גזלה או אפי' יש לו עדים שדר בו המוכר יום אחד אלא שיש למערער עדים שהוחזק המוכר גזלן על שדה זו וגזלן אין לו חזקה והביא המחזיק עדים שנתייעץ עם המערער אם יקחנה ויעצו לקנותה וטוען זה אלו היתה גזולה ממך למה יעצתני לקנותה אינה טענה שיאמר המערער אתה נוח לי להוציאה מידך יותר ממה שאוציאנה מיד הגזלן אבל אם כופר ואומר מעולם לא יעצתיך לקנותה וזה מביא עדים שיעצו מחייבים למערער:
mechaber.en: If he did not bring witnesses. That one day the seller says that the seller is poisoned or an epith has witnessed that the seller has one day, but there is witness to the appellant that the seller is holding on this field and that he does not have a strong one and has brought witnesses that he will advise the appellant if he is forced to buy it, and this claim would have been deprived of you to buy a claim that he will not say that he will be aggressive to me

baer_hetev.he: מחייבים. נרא' דאפילו אם אחר שבאו עדים הודה ואמר שמפני דהשני נוח לי יעצו לא מהני כיון שכבר כפר ולא אמרינן בזה מילי דכדי לא דכירי אינשי. שם:
baer_hetev.en: Required. Nora D even if someone who came to the witnesses confessed and said that the face of the Dasni was comfortable for me would not be the one who had already been a village and did not say this to me. Name:

beer_hagolah.he:
שם פכ"ט עובדא שם לקמיה דרבא שם בריש העמוד ובפירש הרשב"ם שם:
כפי' התוס' שם:
כל כה"ג דלא עביד מעשה אבל עביד מעשה לא אמרינן הכי כדאמרינן בריש סימן קמ"ז וכתב הסמ"ע מ"מ נראה ☜דלא שפיר עביד שנתן לו עצה לטובתו ומכשילו ומציל ממון שלו בממון חבירו ועל כזה קראו חז"ל הא דכתיב לפני עור לא תתן מכשול ולא תשגה עור בדרך:
שם בשם ה"ר יונה וכן כתב הרב המגיד שם בפט"ו דין ג' בשם הרשב"א
beer_hagolah.en:
There, chapter 15, from the incident before Rava at the beginning of the page, according to Rashbam there.
According to Tosafot there.
In every such case where he merely spoke and did no act, we apply this rule. But if he performed an act, we do not, as stated at the beginning of siman 147. Sema writes that nevertheless he acted improperly by giving the other party advice for his own benefit, causing him to stumble and saving his own money at another's expense. To such conduct Chazal applied the verses, "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind," and "Do not mislead the blind on the road."
There, in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah. Maggid Mishneh likewise writes in chapter 15, law 3, in the name of Rashba.

beur_hagra.he: אבל אם כופר. כנ"ל סי"ו ואפי' חוזר וטוען אתה נוח כנ"ל סי"ד:
beur_hagra.en: But if a ransom. The same goes back and says you are comfortable as C.D.:

meirat_einayim.he:
אתה נוח לי. דוקא כל כה"ג דלא עביד מעש' אבל עביד מעש' לא אמרי' הכי כדאמרי בר"ס קמ"ז:
נוח לי כו'. כהנה רבות בהתלמוד ובפוסקים דמהני טענ' זו לדינא ☜ מ"מ נראה דלא שפיר עבד שנתן לו עצה לטובתו ומכשילו ומציל ממון שלו בממון חבירו ועל כזה יקראו חז"ל הא דכתיב לפני עור לא תתן מכשול ולא תשגה עור בדרך:
אבל אם כופר כו' "עד וזה מביא עדים שיעצו כו' נראה דאפילו אם אחר שבאו עדים הודה ואמר שמפני דהשני נוח לי יעצו לא מהני כיון שכבר כפר ולא אמרי' בזה מילי דכדי לא דכירי אינשי ועפ"ר:
meirat_einayim.en:
You are more convenient for me. This type of argument is effective only where the person has not performed an affirmative act. If he did perform an act, we do not accept such an explanation, as stated at the beginning of siman 147.
You are more convenient for me, etc. There are many instances in the Gemara and poskim where such an argument is legally effective. Nevertheless, in my view he did not act properly by advising another person in a way that benefits himself while causing that person to stumble and saving his own money through another person's money. Concerning conduct of this sort the Sages apply the verses, 'You shall not place a stumbling block before the blind,' and, 'You shall not mislead a blind person on the road.'
But if he is a buffer "until and this brings witness to the fact that they will be called," he says, "if others who have come to the witnesses have confessed," and he said, "I will not give up what is already a village, and I will not say," in order to do not reject any of the Inshi and Dr

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: אתה נוח לי. עש"ך בסי' ש"ו ס"ק י"ב שהביא קושית המרדכי מהא דמרא' דינר לשולחני ונמצא דע דחייב משם דיני דגרמי וע"ש מה שתירץ:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: You are more convenient for me. See Shach in siman 306, seif katan 12, where he cites Mordechai's question from one who shows a coin to a money changer and the money changer mistakenly declares it good, who is liable under dina d'garmi. See there for the answer.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
אתה נוח לי כיון דלא עביד מעשה משא"כ בסי' קמ"ז ואפי' לא טען כן טענינן ליה ומ"מ לאו שפיר עבד דעבר אלפני עור [סמ"ע]:
וזה מביא עדים ואפי' אם הודה אחר שבאו עדים וטוען שיעצו משום דהשני נוח לו לא מהני דזה לא הוי מילי דכדי והוחזק כפרן [סמ"ע]:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
"You are comfortable with me because John Dalaid did not say so," he said, "and from the mouths of Lao Shafir," he said
And it brings witnesses and Afi if he admits that he has come to witness and claims that he will be rescued because he is uncomfortable for him, and that he will not be vindicated and held as a victim

pitchei_teshuva.he: ויעצו לקנותה. עיין בתשובת הראנ"ח ח"ב סימן מ"ג שכתב דדוקא בדיבור בעלמא לא איבד זכותו אבל אם היה המערער סרסור ביניהם איבד זכותו דהוי כחותם עליה בעד [בר"ס שאח"ז] כיון דעביד מעשה אך דוקא אם יש עדים שנעשה סרסור אבל אם המחזיק טוען שנעשה סרסור והמערער כופר אינו נאמן במגו דמינך זבינתיה כיון שהחזיק ג"ש דטענת היותו סרסור אינו מקנה לו החזקה עד שנאמר שטענתו אמת וזכה בקרקע אלא הוא ראיה שאין לו זכות בה דאל"כ לא היה מסייע בקנין ואין להביא ראיה ע"פ דבריו של בע"ד ע"ש ועי' בס' שער משפט שהביאו וכ' עליו וז"ל ולא הבנתי דבריו דלמה לא יועיל מגו בכה"ג כיון דלפי דבריו שהמערער נעשה סרסור הרי יש ראיה דמסתמא המערער מכר השדה למי שמכר לו ודמיא לההיא דסי' קמ"ט סט"ז בבא מחמת עו"ג ואמר בפני זבנה מינך או היה לו שטר דנאמן במגו דאני לקחתי ממך שוב מצאתי בתשובות מבי"ט ח"ב סימן רי"ד שכתב להדיא כדברי עכ"ל:
pitchei_teshuva.en: And advised him to purchase it. Responsa Raanach, part 2, siman 43, writes that mere verbal advice does not cause the challenger to lose his rights, but if the challenger actually served as broker between the parties he does lose them, for this is an affirmative act comparable to signing as a witness on the transaction. This applies where there are witnesses that he acted as broker. If the possessor merely claims that the challenger was the broker and the challenger denies it, Raanach says the possessor is not believed by a migo that he could have said, 'I purchased it from you,' because the brokerage claim itself does not create title; it is only evidence that the challenger has no right, since otherwise he would not have assisted in the acquisition, and evidence cannot be created solely from the litigant's own statement. Shaar Mishpat disagrees: once the possessor's version that the challenger acted as broker would ordinarily show that the challenger sold the property to the possessor's seller, why should a migo not validate that account? He compares it to the case where one comes through a non-Jew and says, 'He purchased it from you in my presence,' or has a deed, and is believed by a migo that he himself purchased from the challenger. He later found that Responsa Mabit expressly supports this view.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: שיאמר המערער אתה נח לי וכו' עיין סמ"ע ס"ק ט"ל דמכל מקום שלא כדין עשה והנה ברמב"ם כתב שאמר לו לך קנה השדה טובה היא וכו' ונראה דהעצה היא אם שדה טובה שמנה או רזה אבל אם העצה היה אם השדה בטוח שהוא של מוכר או לא והלא אמר ליה שהוא של מוכר ולקחה עפ"י דבורו נראה דהוי כמראה דינר לחנוני בא"ל עלי דידך קסמכינא ועיין לעיל סימן קכ"ט סעיף ב' ומ"ש שם. וכך כתב בתשובת מהרי"ט חלק חושן משפט סימן ח"י אלא דהוא נתן טעם גם כן דהודאה הוי כמעשה ובזה יש מקום ספק אבל מטעם זה דהוי כמראה דינר לחטני יש לחייבו אם עליו קסמיך כנ"ל. מיהו הראיה שהביא המהרי"ט דהודאה הוי כמעשה מדברי תו' דכתובות דף ק"ט ד"ה אדמון וכו' דהא דאמרינן ראובן אין מעיד ללוי משום דהשני נח לי' יתכן אף לרבנן דהתם לאו הודאה היא משמע אלו הוי הודאה לא אתי' לרבנן ש"מ דהידאה קרוימעשה לרבנן יש לדחות דהתם דמעיד בב"ד פשיטא דהוי מעשה והא לוקין על עדותו אם העיד בשקר ש"מ דעדותו קרוי מעשה וא"כ זה דהעיד בשביל דהשני נח ליה הוי מעשה גמור ולכך תי' התוס' דלא הוי הודאה אבל הודאה בינו לבין בעל דין שלא בבית דין אפשר דלא היי מעשה ואין מהתו' ראי' כלל:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: The challenger may say: you were more convenient for me, etc. See Sema, seif katan 39, who writes that nevertheless the challenger acted improperly. The Rambam's formulation is that the challenger told the purchaser, "go buy the field, it is a good field," which appears to mean that he advised him regarding the quality of the field, whether fertile or poor. But if the advice concerned whether the seller's title was secure, and the challenger told him affirmatively that the field belonged to the seller, so that the purchaser bought in reliance on that statement, it appears that the challenger may be liable. This resembles one who shows a coin to a money changer and says, "I rely on you," as discussed above in siman 129 seif 2 and what I wrote there. Maharit, Choshen Mishpat responsum 18, writes similarly. Maharit also gives the reason that an admission can be treated as an act. There is room to doubt that latter ground, but the reliance principle of showing a coin to a money changer provides a strong basis for liability where the purchaser expressly relied on him. Maharit supports his proposition that an admission is considered an act from Tosafot in Ketubot 109, who discuss the rule that Reuven cannot testify for Levi because the second litigant is more convenient for him. Tosafot say that this can accord even with the Rabbis there because the statement at issue is not an admission, implying that if it were an admission the Rabbis would agree that it creates legal consequences. Maharit infers that an admission is treated as an act. This proof can be rejected. There the person actually testifies in beit din. Testimony in beit din is plainly a legal act. A witness can even receive lashes for false testimony, demonstrating that his testimony is treated as operative conduct. Thus, where he testifies because the second litigant is more convenient for him, that testimony itself is an act. Tosafot therefore need to say that the particular statement is not an admission. But an informal admission made privately to the other party outside beit din may not have the same status. Tosafot therefore provide no proof on that point.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: א"צ למחות כ' הסמ"ע וז"ל שם סיים בטעמא שהרי אין הלוקח מחזיק בה בטענה שקנהו מהמערער אלא וכו' מוכח מזה דהא דכתב א"צ לעשות מחאה בהלוקח היינו דוקא כשהוא מובטח בהלוקח שלא ישקר לטעון שקנהו מהמערער או שהודה הלוקח כן בפני עדים דאל"כ צריך לעשות מחאה שלא יטעון שהמערער לקחוהו ויש לו עידי חזקה סמ"ע ועיין תומים שכתבתי דכוונת הסמ"ע רק לעצה טובה אבל אם עשה כן והלוקח לא טען ממך לקחתי לא איבד המערער זכותו דהא עכ"פ לראשון מיחה והשני מודה שלא לקחו ממנו וזה ברור ונכון ודלא כמהרי"ט בתשובה הנ"ל שהשיג על הסמ"ע שדעתו דס"ל לסמ"ע דאיבד זכותו אבל לא כן הוא:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: He need not protest. Sema cites the source: the later purchaser does not claim that he bought from the challenger, but only that he acquired through the prior possessor. This suggests that if the challenger is not confident the later purchaser will admit that chain, prudence favors making a protest. See Tumim. This is advice, not an absolute legal requirement. If the challenger did not protest and the later purchaser never claims purchase directly from him, the challenger's right is not lost because he did protest against the first possessor and the later purchaser admits he did not buy directly from him. This is unlike Maharit, who misunderstood Sema as making nonprotest an automatic forfeiture.

mechaber.he: אם הביא המחזיק עדים שא"ל המערער לקחתה לו מיד המוכר אינה טענה לומר לו אם הוא שלך למה רצית לקנות דעביד אינש דזבין דיניה: הגה מי שקנה קרקע אחת שני פעמים ותובע המוכר במעות השניים אם טוען המוכר שחזר ולקחה מן הלוקח ולכן חזר ומכרה לו שנית נאמן ואם אינו טוען כך צריך הלוקח לברר למה קנאה שני פעמים אם אמר שטעה נאמן ואם אמר שידע ולקחה שני פעמים הדין עם המוכר דודאי נתן לו המעות לשם מתנה (ב"י בשם הרשב"א):
mechaber.en: If the holder brought witnesses that the Appellant took him immediately, the seller did not say to him if he was yours, why you wanted to buy an employer Izzbin of her law: He who bought one land two times and was sued by the two bubbles if he claims that the seller came back and took him a loyal second, and if he does not claim that he should find out why he was jealous two times if he was wrong

baer_hetev.he:
הביאו. ע"ל סי' קמ"ב סס"א ובתשו' מהרשד"ם סי' שכ"ד:
מתנה. כמו שאמרו בפ"ק דב"מ גבי הכיר בה שאינה שלו ולקחה ובמקדש אחותו דאיפליגו רב ושמואל דהלכ' כשמואל עכ"ל תשובת הרשב"א שבב"י ותמוה לי דהא אסיק רבא שם דהלכתא מעות יש לו והיינו דלא כשמואל וכ"פ כל הפוסקים וכמ"ש בסי' שע"ג ואע"ג דלגבי מקדש אחותו קי"ל דאין המעות חוזרים וכמ"ש בא"ע סי' נ' והיינו מטעם שכתב הה"מ דקי"ל כשמואל בדיני שאני התם וכמ"ש הרא"ש פ"ק דב"מ וז"ל מהא דפסק רבא דמעות יש לו אין לדקדק דהלכה כרב במקדש אחותו דדלמא שאני בין אחותו לנוכראה ע"כ וכה"ג מחלקים בש"ס שם ודוחק לומר דשאני הכא כיון דהכיר בה שאינה שלו אלא של עצמו אפי' רבא מודה ועוד דא"כ לא היה צריך הרשב"א לו' דהלכה כשמואל דהא כיון דרבא מודה א"כ גם רב מודה וצ"ע עכ"ל הש"ך:
baer_hetev.en:
brought. According to S. C. C. K.C., “And I will be like this.”
A gift. This is like what the Sages said in the first chapter of Bava Metzia regarding one who knowingly purchased property that did not belong to the seller, and regarding one who betrothed his sister, where Rav and Shmuel disagree and the halachah is said to follow Shmuel. These are the words of the Rashba's responsum cited by the Beit Yosef. This is difficult, for Rava concludes there that the purchaser is entitled to recover his money, which is contrary to Shmuel, and all the authorities rule accordingly, as stated in siman 373. Although regarding one who betroths his sister we rule that the money is not returned, as stated in Even HaEzer siman 50, based on the Maggid Mishneh's explanation that we follow Shmuel in monetary law, that case is different. The Rosh likewise writes in the first chapter of Bava Metzia that Rava's ruling that the purchaser recovers his money does not prove that the halachah follows Rav regarding one who betroths his sister, because there may be a distinction between his sister and an unrelated woman. Similar distinctions appear in the Gemara there. It is strained to say that here, since he knew the property was not the seller's but his own, even Rava agrees. Moreover, if so the Rashba would not have needed to say that the halachah follows Shmuel, because if Rava agrees then Rav would agree as well. This requires study. Shach.

beer_hagolah.he:
שם סעיף ל' נלמד מדין עובדא דלעיל מ"ש בסיף ט"ז:
פי' לקנות קרקע הראוי לו בדמים מועטים ולא לטרוח ולבא בדין רשב"ם ופי' ר"ח קונה אותם הדינים והמריבות באותם דמים:
beer_hagolah.en:
The name of section L. is taught from an employee who is a member of the High Court of Justice:
P. To buy land that is worthy of little fabrics, and not to bother and come in the Law of Rashi and P.R. buys them in the same manner:

beur_hagra.he:
אם הביא. שם כפי' הרשב"ם:
אם טוען המוכר. כתובות פח א' אכתי יכולה כו':
ואם אין. שם כגי' הראשונים דמודה להו:
אם אמר שטעה. כמו לא הכיר בה שאינה שלו דלד"ה מעות יש לו. ב"מ יג ב':
ואם אמר שידע. דהוי כמו הכיר. שם י"ד ב' דלשמואל המעות מתנה וצ"ע דקי"ל שם כרב ועש"ך:
beur_hagra.en:
If he brought... This follows Rashbam's explanation there.
If the seller claims. Kesubos 88a, "She can still..."
If there is no... According to the reading of the early authorities that he admits to them.
If he says he erred. This is like one who sold property he did not know was not his, where everyone agrees that he recovers his money, Bava Metzia 13b.
If he says he knew. This resembles one who knowingly bought property not belonging to the seller. According to Shmuel, the money is a gift. This requires study because we rule there like Rav. See Shach.

meirat_einayim.he:
שא"ל המערער לקחת' לו מיד המוכר. בטור כ' לקחנ' לו מיד המוכר:
דעביד אינש דזבין דיני'. וע"ל סי' קמ"ב סס"א מ"ש בזה:
ולכן חזר ומכרו לו שנית נאמן ז"ל התשובה שם "נאמן מאחר שראובן עשה מעש' וקנאו ממנו זו ראיה גמורה שחזר ומכרה לו ול"ד להא דאמרי' דעביד אינש דזבין דיני' דהתם באינו חוזר ותובע המעות מיירי כו' ע"ש:
ואם אינו טוען כן פי' אלא טוען ודאי למתנה כוון הלוקח כיון שנתנה לו שנית וצ"ל דמיירי שידוע שקנא' שני פעמים ודו"ק:
meirat_einayim.en:
He was asked to take him right away. In the column, he is immediately known:
"Indeed, Izin is debating the law." And then, he said, “I will give you a lot.”
And therefore he returned and sold it to him a second time, he is believed. The responsum states: He is believed, because Reuven performed an affirmative act and bought it from him. This is complete proof that the other person had sold it back to him. This is not comparable to the rule that a person may pay money merely to buy off litigation, because that rule concerns a case where he does not later return and demand the money. See there.
And if he does not say yes, he is certainly a gift that he has given him a second, and that he is known to be jealous of two times

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: לשום מתנה עש"ך סקי"ז שתמה ע"ז דהא אנן קי"יל כרב דהמעו' פקדון ע"ש ולפענ"ד נראה דדעת הרב הוא דכאן כ"ע מודים דליכא למיחש לפקדון דגרע מהא דאמרינן ביבמות ד' קט"ו כיון דשמיה כשמיה לא מפקיד גבי והיינו משום דיהיה נאמן לטעון שהוא שלו וא"כ הכא כיון דנתן להמוכר המעות בשם מכירה לפני עדים ואז המוכר נאמן על כל טענה שירצה כמ"ש הרב ואפי' שבוע' א"צ וגם אפי' אם יש לו איזה טענה שאינו זוכה בדין יכול הוא לומ' דזבין דיני' ובכה"ג ודאי לא מפקיד גביה וע"כ משום מתנה נתן לו משא"כ בהכיר בו שאינו שלו או במקדש אחותו דבודאי יתחייב להחזיר ושום טענה לא יועיל ואפי' החזרתי לא תהיה אחותו המתקדשת יכולת לטעון כיון שקיבלה לשם קידושין וכיון דשמואל סבר לשם מתנה שייך לומר מי יימר דמחייבי לי רבנן ולכך אמרי' דגמר ונתן לשם פקדון ולבסוף יתבעהו להחזיר לו והנה בתומים כ' דאם קיבל אחריות לא הוי מתנה כמ"ש התו' בב"מ ט"ו ע"ב ד"ה מעות יש לו לענין הכיר בו שאינו שלו וה"נ דכוותיה ולפענ"ד לא דמי כלל דבשלמא בהכיר בו שאינו שלו איכ' חיוב אחריו' על המוכר שאם יטרפו ממני יתחייב לשלם שופר' שבחא ופירי וי"ל שלא נתן לו לשם מתנה רק לשם תועלת האחריות דשבחא ופירי וגם יש לו תועלת להלוקח באכילת פירו' עד שיבוא הטורף משא"כ במכר את אשר הוא שלו לגמרי שאין להלוקח שום תועלת בחיוב אחריו של המוכר וגם בהמוכר אין עליו שום חיוב בקבלת אחריות נגד מי שהשד' שלו לגמרי ולכך סתמו הפוסקי' וכתבו דהוי מתנה בכל ענין ובהא דפסק הרב שנאמן לומר שטעה אף דבכ"מ טעיתי טענה גרועה היא הכא שאני כיון דהמוכר בעצמו מודה שאין לו שום טענה סברא הוא שטעה ולפ"ז אם המוכר אומר שהי' לו איזה טענה אף שאינו זוכה בדין לפי טענה ההיא וטוען שנתן לו המעות מחמת שרצה לקנו' דינו נאמן המוכר ואין הלוקח נאמן לומר טעיתי שהיא טענה גרועה ועסמ"ע סקמ"ד מ"ש דמיירי שידוע שקנאה ב"פ והוא תמוה דאפי' במודה והלה טוען שטעה סגי דל"ש מגו שאין טוען ברי שנתנה במתנה וגם א"ל דקאי ארישא בטוען חזר ולקחה שכ' בס"ק מ"ג טעם למה נאמן ולזה כתב דמיירי בידוע דבמודה בלאו הטעם מהימן במגו אמנם גם בזוז קשה דהא בעינן הטעם לענין דל"צ שבועה דמטעם מגו בעי שבועה:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: As a gift. See Shach, seif katan 17, who questions this because we rule like Rav that the money is a deposit. In my view, Rama holds that here everyone agrees there is no concern that it was deposited. Yevamot 115 says that when one man's name is the same as another's, the first does not deposit money with him, because the second could later claim that the money is his. Here the purchaser gave the seller money before witnesses specifically as the price of a sale, and at that point the seller was believed on any claim he might make, as Rama writes. He need not even swear. Even if he had some claim that would not legally establish ownership, he could say that he bought the right to litigate. In such circumstances no one would entrust money to him merely as a deposit. The money must therefore have been given as a gift. This differs from one who knowingly buys property that is not the seller's, or one who gives kiddushin money to his sister. There the seller or recipient will certainly be obligated to return the money, and no alternative claim can save her. Even a claim of return would not help the sister, because she received it expressly for kiddushin. Since Shmuel holds that in such a case the money may have been a gift, the other opinion can reasonably say that perhaps the payer intended it as a deposit until he later sought return. Tumim writes that if the seller accepted warranty, the money cannot be considered a gift, comparing this to Tosafot in Bava Metzia 15 regarding a purchaser who knowingly buys property not belonging to the seller. In my view this is not comparable. There the seller's warranty gives the purchaser a real benefit if the land is taken from him, because the seller becomes liable for improvement, produce, and related losses. The purchaser also benefits from using the produce until dispossession. One can therefore say that he paid for those benefits rather than making a gift. Here, however, the purchaser buys what already belongs entirely to the seller. The purchaser receives no benefit at all from the warranty, and the seller has no separate obligation under the warranty to the person who actually owns the field. Therefore the poskim state without qualification that the money is a gift. As to Rama's ruling that the purchaser is believed to say that he made a mistake, although "I was mistaken" is generally a weak claim, here it is different because the seller himself admits that he had no legal basis at all. It is reasonable that the purchaser erred. If, however, the seller says that he had some arguable right, even one insufficient to prevail in law, and claims that the purchaser paid in order to acquire that litigation right, the seller is believed and the purchaser cannot prevail merely by saying, "I was mistaken," for that is a weak claim. See Sema, seif katan 44. His statement that the case concerns one where it is known that the purchaser bought twice is difficult. An admission by the seller together with the purchaser's mistake claim should suffice, because there is no migo where the purchaser cannot definitely claim that the money was a gift. Nor can Sema's remark be read merely as addressing the earlier clause in which the seller claims that he later repurchased the land. Even there the stated reason remains necessary to explain why no oath is required, since a migo alone would still require an oath.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
דעביד איניש דזבין דיניה. ודוקא אם טען אבל אנן לא טענינין כן עבורו [סמ"ע]:
ומכרה לו שנית נאמן מאחר שעשה מעשה וקנאה ממנו זהו ראיה גמורה שחזר ומכרה לו [סמ"ע].
לשם מתנה ותמיה דהא קי"ל בסי' שע"ג גבי הכיר בה שאינו שלו דהלכה כרב דהמעות פקדון ודוחק נומר דשאכי הכא כיון שהוא של עצמו [ש"ך] וע"ב:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
I am afraid of the law. And if he said, “I am not a fool.”
And he sold him again faithfully because he made an act of envy from him, it was a complete evidence that he had returned and sold him.
As a gift. This is surprising, because in siman 373 concerning one who knowingly buys property that is not the seller's, we rule like Rav that the purchase money is held as a deposit. It is strained to distinguish our case merely because the property is actually his own. Shach. See Beurim.

siftei_kohen.he:
[" אם הביא המחזיק עדים כו'. עיין בתשובת מהרשד\"ם סימן שכ\"ד:"]
[" לשם מתנה. וכמו שאמרו בפ\"ק דמציעא גבי הכיר בה שאינה שלו ולקחה ובמקדש את אחותו דאיפלגו רב ושמואל דהלכה כשמואל עכ\"ל תשובות רשב\"א שבבית יוסף ותמי' לי דהא אסיק רבא בפ\"ק דמציעא שם דהלכתא מעות יש לו והיינו דלא כשמואל וכ\"פ כל הפוסקים וכדלקמן סי' שע\"ג ואע\"ג דלגבי מקדש אחותו קי\"ל דאין המעות חוזרים וכמ\"ש הרמב\"ם והמחבר בא\"ע סי' נ' והיינו מטעם שכ' הרב המגיד דקי\"ל כשמואל בדינא שאני התם וכמ\"ש הרא\"ש פ\"ק דמציעא וז\"ל מהא דפסק רבא דמעות יש לו אין לדקדק דהלכה כרב במקדש אחותו דדילמא שאני בין אחותו לנוכראה עכ\"ל וכה\"ג מחלקים בש\"ס שם ודוחק לומר דשאני הכא כיון דהכיר בה שאינה שלו אלא של עצמו אפי' רבא מודה ועוד דאם כן לא היה צריך הרשב\"א לומר דהלכה כשמואל דהא כיון דרבא מודה אם כן גם רב מודה וצ\"ע:"]
siftei_kohen.en:
[If the owner brought witnesses. See the answer from the radar
As a gift. The Rashba's responsum cited by the Beit Yosef compares this to the cases in the first chapter of Bava Metzia where one knowingly purchases property that is not the seller's, and where one betroths his sister. Rav and Shmuel dispute those cases, and the responsum states that the law follows Shmuel. This is difficult, because Rava concludes in Bava Metzia that the purchaser recovers his money, contrary to Shmuel, and all the authorities rule accordingly, as stated below in siman 373. Although in the case of one who betroths his sister we rule that the money is not returned, as Rambam and the Mechaber state in Even HaEzer, siman 50, Maggid Mishneh explains that this follows Shmuel only in that distinct context. The Rosh likewise writes that Rava's ruling does not establish the law as Rav in the case of betrothing one's sister, because there may be a distinction between one's sister and an unrelated woman. The Gemara itself draws such distinctions. It is difficult to say that here, because he knew the property was not the seller's but his own, even Rava would agree, for then the Rashba would not have needed to invoke the ruling like Shmuel, and Rav too would agree. This requires study. Citation references: 100, 370.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
דודאי נתן וכו' מתנה הש"ך ס"ק חו"ב תמה דהרשב"א יליף זה דהלכה כשמואל דמעות לשם מתנה דהא קיימא לן בהכיר בו שאינו שלו דהמעות פקדון לקמן בסי' שע"ג רק גבי מקדש אחותו קיימא לן בא"ע סימן נו"ן דמעות מתנה ובזו כבר כתב הרא"ש הטעם משום דהוה ליה אחותו עיין שם ונראה דהרשב"א סבירא ליה א"כ הקונה שדה מאחיו והכיר בו שאינה שלו יהיה המעות מתנה מ"ש אחיו ומ"ש אחותו ודבר זה לא שמענו בשום פוסק ועוד דא"כ למה פליגי בקדושי אחותו והכי' בו שאינו שלו ולקח' לפליגי בהכיר בו שאינו שלו ולקח' מאחיו או מאחר דלרב פקדון ולשמואל מתנה וכן בקדושי אחותו דאם נאמר הטעם לכך מתנה משום דהואיל דהיא אחותו א"כ המקדש שארי נשים שאין קידושין תופסין בהו כגון אשת איש ושפחה וכדומה יהיה קידושין לפקדון משום דהם נכרים לו וזהו גם כן דלא מצינו חילוק בהו בפוסקים והרמב"ם פרק ו' מהלכות זכי' כתב שהכל יודעים שאין קידושין תופסין בעריות הרי משמע דבכל עריות דינא הכי וכן נראה מדברי המגיד משנה שם דוקא בקדושי טעות הקדושין חוזרין ולא זולתו וגם בזה א"ל תרתי פלוגתא הל"ל המקדש אחותו או שפחה רב אמר פקדון ושמואל אומר מתנה ושמעינן גם כן תרתי מיניה ול"ל למימר בפקדון ואף זה כמוהו ודברי רשב"א נכונים ומוכרחים בגמרא ובפוסקים:

urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
For he certainly gave it, etc., as a gift. The Shach in seif katan 22 questions the Rashba's derivation that the halachah follows Shmuel, who treats the money as a gift. After all, below in siman 373 we rule that where a buyer knew the property was not the seller's, the money is treated as a deposit, whereas only regarding one who betroths his own sister do we rule in Even HaEzer siman 50 that the money is a gift. The Rosh already explains that rule by the special fact that she is his sister. It appears that the Rashba reasoned differently. If kinship alone were decisive, then one who knowingly buys a field from his brother even though it is not the brother's should likewise be treated as having given the purchase money as a gift. Why distinguish brother from sister? No authority states such a rule. Moreover, if kinship were the reason, why do Rav and Shmuel formulate their dispute separately concerning betrothing one's sister and concerning knowingly buying property that does not belong to the seller? They could have disputed a single intermediate case, such as one who knowingly buys another's property from his brother versus from a stranger, from which both principles could be learned. Likewise, if the gift result in betrothing one's sister depends only on her being his sister, then where a man gives kiddushin to another woman with whom kiddushin cannot take effect, such as a married woman or a maidservant, the money should be treated as a deposit because she is unrelated to him. Yet the authorities do not draw such a distinction. The Rambam in chapter 6 of Hilchot Zechiyah writes that everyone knows kiddushin do not take effect with forbidden relations, implying that the same rule applies generally to all such forbidden women. The Maggid Mishneh likewise indicates that only in ordinary mistaken kiddushin is the money returned, not in these cases. Here too, if kinship were essential, the Gemara could have framed Rav and Shmuel's dispute as one who betroths his sister or a maidservant, thereby teaching both distinctions together. The Rashba therefore holds that wherever there is a plausible reason other than gift, we prefer it, because why should a person give away his property without cause? A person is naturally protective of his own property, and in this sense everyone is like a stranger to him. The Gemara's phrase that people do not simply give gifts to strangers expresses this general presumption, not a technical distinction between relatives and strangers. In the case of betrothing one's sister, however, no plausible non-gift purpose exists. It is difficult to say that he intended a deposit. There are many trustworthy people in the world with whom he could deposit money. Why would he specifically hand it to his sister under the guise of kiddushin? Therefore Shmuel says he must have intended a gift. By contrast, where one knowingly buys property that does not belong to the seller, there is a clear reason to classify the payment as a deposit connected to a real transaction. Meanwhile the buyer is using the field and consuming its produce as though it were his. If the true owner never appears, the buyer may effectively continue benefiting from it, and the seller cannot simply eject him. The Gemara and Rosh indicate as much. Even in an ordinary sale Shmuel holds that a person may knowingly purchase land for only a day. All the more so here, where the money will ultimately be returned if the true owner successfully claims the field. The buyer therefore gains useful possession in the meantime. We have no reason to assume an outright gift, especially because the presumption is that a person does not gratuitously give his money away. In kiddushin that cannot take effect, by contrast, the giver receives no practical benefit from treating the payment as a deposit under the guise of kiddushin. Therefore we say that he intended a gift. The Rashba's reasoning is thus sound, even if the Gemara's word "strangers" is somewhat imprecise in this broader sense. The same applies in the present case, where a person purchases what is already his. He gains nothing through the purchase because he would in any event remain in possession indefinitely, since the property is his. The case therefore closely resembles giving kiddushin to a woman with whom kiddushin cannot take effect. We rule like Shmuel that the money is a gift because no meaningful deposit purpose exists. The Rashba's words are thus well founded in the Gemara and the authorities.
Now, all of this refers to a case where the buyer did not expressly receive warranty at the time of the transaction. If the seller expressly accepted warranty, even Shmuel, who treats the money as a gift where the buyer knew the property was not the seller's, agrees that the payment is not a gift. Tosafot in Bava Metzia 17b write this, and the Rashba himself writes it later at length. The same applies here. How could one regard the money as a gift where the recipient expressly accepted liability to reimburse? The case must therefore be one of an ordinary transaction without explicit warranty. Although we generally rule that warranty is presumed even if omitted, that principle applies where the buyer did not know the defect. Where he knew the property was already his, as here, his payment is conclusively given as a gift absent an express warranty. This is clear and correct.

urim_vetumim_urim.en: If he brings witnesses, it returns. Tur says the claimant swears and takes. Mechaber follows Rambam, who does not mention an oath. Above at the beginning of siman 140 Mechaber did require an oath in the ordinary case where a possessor claims purchase without three years' possession. Sema suggests Mechaber relied here on that earlier rule, though he also notes a distinction. The Shach says the claimant is like one who extracts land and therefore should swear even on an uncertain defense, but this is not convincing. See Tumim. In my view even Tur agrees no oath is needed merely to recover the land. The oath concerns produce the claimant seeks to recover, because perhaps he had sold the land to another person and may be liable to repay the produce again, as explained above in siman 145:7. This is clearer than Sema and Shach.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: That he consumed it for seven years. See Sema, seif katan 46, through his statement that so long as the claimant does not prove that the seller lived there for one day. urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
ויש לו עדים שדר בו המוכר יום א' עיין סמ"ע שכ' שא"צ דהא המערער מודה שדר בו דהא לקחה הימנו אלא שמעשה היה כך הי'. ועיין ש"ך ס"ק ח"י שכ' דליתא בגמרא שהיה מעשה כך. ובאמת כוונת הסמ"ע כך דע"כ זה שבא על המחזיק מה בעית בהאי שדה ע"כ דלא בא בשטרו דא"כ הא כתב הטור וכן הש"ע בסעיף כ"א דאם נודע למחזיק שהמערער בא בשטרו א"צ שבע שנים דיש לו מגו ממך לקחתי וא"כ יש להבין באיזה טענה בא עד שהמחזיק נזקק להשיב לו ולא השיבו מי את שאשיב לך ומה איכפת לך בקרקע זו וא"כ ישיב לכל אדם ענינו ועכצ"ל דגם למערער היה חזקת אבות רק האמת דמוכר של המחזיק לקחו מאבותיו והוא המערער בא בשטרו שלקחו אח"כ מיד המוכר ולכך מתחילה בא בעידי אבות וכשהשיב לו שלקחו מהמוכר בא בשטר קנינו וא"כ שזה מתחילה בא בעדי אבות וזהו השיבו דלקחו מהמוכר ע"כ הוצרך להביא עדים שדר בו יום אחד דאל"כ מה יועיל חזקתו ובמגו דממך לקחתי אינו נאמן על דר בו חד יומא כמ"ש הטור והרז"ה ורמב"ן ועיין לעיל סעיף י"ד וכמ"ש הש"ך ומש"ל בזה. ואם המערער מודה דדר בו המוכר יום אחד הרי יש למערער מגו דלא דר בו המוכר וכשאומר שדר רק לקחה הימנו נאמן וא"צ שטר ולמה הצריך דוקא שטר ומגו להוציא לא הוה דכיון דגם הוא יש לו חזקת אבות כמש"ל וא"ש ודוק:
אבל אם אכלה פחות מז' שנים וכו' עיין ש"ך ס"ק י"ט דמפרש דאף דשטר אית ליה קלא ויודע ודאי דלקחה בשטר אין להשטר קול על פלוני שלקחה רק סתם שלקחה אחד אבל לא נודע לו מי לקחה. ויותר מסתברים דברי הסמ"ע לעיל סי' קמ"ד ס"ק ד' דאף דשטר אית ליה קלא אין זה ודאי ששמעה המחזיק רק הואיל ועשה שלו ומיחה כדינו לא חייבו חכמים יותר ועל המחזיק לחקור ואם לא חקר אפסיד אנפשיה אבל מ"מ מגו לא אמרינן דאולי לא ברור לו כ"כ. ולכך אינו טוען כן ונכון ופשוט. ולדברי הש"ך יש לפקפק במ"ש התוספות דף ל"א ד"ה אבל התי' על קושית ריב"ם כמ"ש הטור וקשה מ"מ יאמן שבאמת אומר שאכל ז' שנים דאל"כ עדיין לא הואיל בטענתו לגבי מוכר דלא יהיה לו נגדו שנין חזקה דהא מיחה דלדעת הש"ך המחאה שמע וא"כ אם אין יודע בנפשו שהאמת שג"ש קודם ששמע המחאה החזיק אף המוכר יוציאנו מידו ול"ל דהא המוכר צריך למחות כל ג"ש ז"א דהא התוספות כתבו בדף ל"ט ע"ב בד"ה וצריך למחות דהך סוגיא לא ס"ל דצריך למחות כל ג"ש ועכצ"ל כסמ"ע דלא שמע כלל אפילו קול דברים וא"כ תושב אם יבא המוכר בזו ג' שנים אחרונים שהחזקתי לא יכול להוציאו מידו כי לא שמע מחאה כלל ודוק:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
And he has witnesses that the seller lived there one day. The Sema writes that such witnesses are unnecessary because the challenger himself admits that the seller lived there, since the challenger claims to have purchased from that seller; the Gemara merely happened to describe the case as having witnesses. The Shach in seif katan 18 writes that the Gemara does not in fact say that this was merely the historical fact of the case. The Sema's intention, however, can be understood as follows. The challenger comes to the present possessor and asks, "what are you doing in this field?" He plainly cannot initially be relying on his purchase deed. If he had already disclosed that deed to the possessor, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in seif 21 rule that the possessor would not need seven years, because he would have a migo to say, "I bought it from you." We must therefore ask: on what basis did the challenger come against the possessor at all? Why did the possessor have to answer him rather than say, "who are you that I should respond to you, and what concern is this field of yours?" The case must be that the challenger also had ancestral title. In truth, the possessor's seller had purchased the field from the challenger's ancestors, while the challenger later acquired it back from that seller. The challenger therefore first comes with witnesses of ancestral title. When the possessor responds that he purchased from the intermediate seller, the challenger then produces his deed showing that he later bought it from that seller. If so, once the challenger first arrives with ancestral-title witnesses and the possessor answers that he acquired from the intermediate seller, the possessor necessarily needs proof that the intermediate seller lived there at least one day. Otherwise the possessor's own chazakah cannot help. He is not believed by a migo that he bought directly from the challenger to establish the seller's one day of residence, as the Tur, Baal HaMaor, and Ramban hold, and as discussed above in seif 14 and in the Shach. If, however, the challenger himself admits that the intermediate seller lived there one day, then the challenger has a migo that he could have denied the seller's residence. By admitting it and saying only that he later purchased from that seller, the challenger should be believed without needing a deed. This is not a migo to extract in the objectionable sense, because the challenger also has ancestral title, as explained above. Why then does the law require specifically a deed? This demonstrates that the Gemara's case indeed involved independent proof of the seller's one-day residence rather than relying simply on the challenger's admission. In this way the Sema's underlying concern can be understood, though the precise historical wording of the Gemara is as the Shach notes.
But if he consumed it for fewer than seven years, etc. See Shach, seif katan 19, who explains that although a deed creates publicity and the possessor certainly knows that the property was sold by deed, the public report does not necessarily identify the particular purchaser. People know that someone bought it, but not who. The Sema's explanation above in siman 144, seif katan 4, is more convincing. Even though a deed creates publicity, it does not mean with certainty that this particular possessor actually heard the report. Rather, the owner did what the law required and protested in the legally effective manner. The Sages did not require more of him. It then became the possessor's responsibility to investigate, and if he failed to do so he caused his own loss. But for purposes of migo, we cannot simply assume with certainty that he knew all the details of the deed. He may genuinely not know them, and therefore his failure to make a particular alternative claim does not create a migo against him. This is simple and correct. According to the Shach, there is difficulty with Tosafot on 31a, who answer Riva's question as the Tur later explains. Even if the possessor does not know the purchaser's identity, why should he not be believed when he says that he truly consumed for seven years? Otherwise his claim would still not protect him against the original seller. The seller's deed itself serves as a protest, and according to the Shach the possessor did hear the general protest. Unless he knows that he had already possessed for three years before that protest, the original seller could still remove him. One cannot answer that the original seller would have needed to renew his protest every three years, because Tosafot on 39b expressly write that the sugya there does not accept the requirement of renewed protest every three years. We must therefore understand the matter like the Sema: the possessor may have heard no report at all, not even a vague one. Thus if the original seller later comes, the possessor can rely on the final three years because he never heard any effective protest. This fits Tosafot and should be preferred.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: א"צ טענה כתב הש"ך דא"צ ראיה היותו יורש או לוקח כיון דהחזיק ג"ש ואומר שהוא יורש או לוקח מהימן וכ"כ הטור בשם הרמב"ן והרא"ש וכ"כ המ"מ ע"ש ועיין תומים שהרשב"א הביא הב"י בס"ז מחודש י"ד ס"ל דווקא אם הוא החזיק ג"ש אבל אם זה שמכרה או הורישה דר בו ג"ש והוא בא מחמתו בטענת מקח ל"א דנאמן דאמרינן אילו היה המחזיק פה היה מודה דלפירות הורידו ע"ש שהסכמתי כן לדינא כי לא נמצא חולק ע"ז אף שבכה"ג הביא קצת מחברים דס"ל דרשב"א חולק על הרמב"ן ורא"ש אבל זה ליתא לכן דברי הרשב"א תבנא לדינא וע"ש:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: He need not make a claim. The Shach writes that he need not even prove that he is an heir or purchaser. If he possessed for three years and says he is an heir or purchaser, he is believed. Tur cites Ramban and Rosh, and Maggid Mishneh agrees. See Tumim. Rashba, however, holds that if the present possessor did not himself possess for three years but relies on the fact that the seller or decedent did, then when he claims through purchase he may need proof that he indeed comes through that predecessor, because perhaps the predecessor would have admitted he held only for produce. I concluded that Rashba's ruling should be accepted, since I found no true dissent from it.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: הביא המחזיק עדים דהודאת פיו שאמר מקודם ג"ש פוסל העדים של הז"ש [סמ"ע]:
